question: The numbers \(1,\) \(2,\) \(\dots,\) \(9\) are randomly placed into the \(9\) squares of a \(3 \times 3\) grid. Each square gets one number, and each of the numbers is used once. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers in each row and each column is odd?
solution:
Only the positions of the odd and even numbers affect whether a sum is odd. There are five odd numbers and four even numbers.

Adding an even number preserves parity and adding an odd number switches it, so a sum is odd exactly when the number of odd summands is odd. A row has an odd sum exactly when it contains one or three odd numbers. Since the three rows together contain five odd numbers, their odd-number counts must be \(3,1,1\). Thus exactly one row is entirely odd. The same reasoning shows that exactly one column is entirely odd.

The all-odd row and all-odd column together occupy
\[
3+3-1=5
\]
cells, using all five odd numbers. The four cells outside their union must therefore contain the even numbers. Conversely, every pattern of this form works: the chosen row and column each contain three odd numbers, and every other row and column contains one.

There are \(3\cdot3=9\) such patterns. None is counted twice because each has a unique all-odd row and a unique all-odd column.

The total number of ways to choose the four even-number positions is
\[
\binom94=\frac{9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6}{4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}=126.
\]
These patterns are equally likely: each allows \(5!\) arrangements of the odd numbers and \(4!\) arrangements of the even numbers. Hence the probability is
\[
\frac{9}{126}=\boxed{\frac1{14}},
\]
choice \(\textbf{B}\).
